title: Find Median from a Data Stream
prompt: Design a data structure that supports two operations on a stream of integers: addNum(num) inserts an integer into the data structure, and findMedian() returns the median of all elements added so far. The median is the middle value of the sorted elements; if the count is even, it's the average of the two middle values. Optimize for many interleaved addNum and findMedian calls.
blurb: The two-heaps classic — a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced so the median is at the tops.

rubric.label: Problem understanding
rubric.description: Understands it's a streaming/online problem with repeated queries, so re-sorting each query is wasteful; median definition for even vs odd counts.

rubric.label: Approach
rubric.description: Reaches the two-heaps design: a max-heap for the lower half, a min-heap for the upper half; median from the tops. Justifies why this beats a sorted array.

rubric.label: Correctness
rubric.description: Maintains the size invariant (heaps differ by at most 1) AND the ordering invariant (every lower <= every upper) on each addNum; findMedian handles odd/even correctly.

rubric.label: Complexity analysis
rubric.description: O(log n) per addNum, O(1) per findMedian, O(n) space; contrasts with sorted-array O(n) insert or O(n log n) re-sort.

rubric.label: Code quality
rubric.description: Clean push-then-rebalance logic; a single, well-defined rebalancing rule rather than scattered conditionals.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: First element, even vs odd counts, all-equal or duplicate values, negatives, integer-overflow-safe averaging of the two middles.

rubric.label: Testing
rubric.description: Interleaves adds and queries verifying the median after each add, including an even-count average.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: States both invariants (size and ordering) explicitly and explains the rebalance step clearly.

constraints: -10^5 <= num <= 10^5 (follow-up relaxes this to a bounded range)
findMedian is only called after at least one addNum
Up to ~5*10^4 calls to addNum and findMedian combined
Averaging two middles must avoid integer overflow (use (a+b)/2.0 or a + (b-a)/2)

examples.explanation: After [1,2] the median is (1+2)/2 = 1.5. After [1,2,3] the median is the middle value 2.0.

reference.optimal_time: O(log n) per addNum, O(1) per findMedian
reference.optimal_space: O(n) to hold all elements across the two heaps

approaches.name: brute force (sorted array, re-sort or insert)
approaches.idea: Keep all numbers; on findMedian sort and pick the middle (O(n log n) per query), or keep a sorted array and binary-search the insert position (O(log n) to find but O(n) to shift for the insert). Fine for few queries, poor for a heavy interleaved stream.
approaches.time: O(n) insert or O(n log n) per query

approaches.name: optimal: two heaps (max-heap low + min-heap high)
approaches.idea: Maintain a max-heap 'low' for the smaller half and a min-heap 'high' for the larger half, with two invariants: (size) len(low) is equal to or one more than len(high); (order) every element in low <= every element in high. addNum: push to low, then move low's max to high (to enforce order), then if high got bigger than low, move high's min back to low (to enforce size). findMedian: if sizes equal, average the two tops; else return low's top (the max-heap root).

approaches.name: balanced BST / order-statistics tree
approaches.idea: An augmented balanced BST (subtree sizes) supports insert in O(log n) and select-kth in O(log n), giving the median directly. More general (supports removal, arbitrary rank) but heavier to implement than two heaps.

approaches.name: bounded-range: counting/bucket histogram
approaches.idea: If values are integers in a small fixed range, keep a count array/Fenwick tree; find the median by prefix-sum walk. O(range) or O(log range) per query.
approaches.time: O(log range) with a Fenwick tree

follow_ups: If all numbers are integers in a small fixed range [0,100], can you do better than O(log n)? (bucket/counting histogram, O(1)-ish).
If ~99% of numbers are in [0,100] with rare outliers, combine a histogram for the common range with heaps/overflow lists for the tails.
Support removeNum(num) as well — heaps make arbitrary removal O(n); switch to two multiset/BST structures with lazy deletion.
Sliding-window median: only the last k elements count — two multisets (or heaps with lazy deletion) keyed to evict the window's departing element.
Distributed stream across many machines — approximate quantiles with t-digest or the Greenwald-Khanna sketch, and why exact medians don't merge cheaply.
reference.reference_solution: State: low = max-heap (store negatives if the language only has a min-heap), high = min-heap. addNum(num): heappush(low, num); // tentatively add to lower half; heappush(high, heappop(low)); // move the largest of low into high to keep order invariant (every low <= every high); if len(high) > len(low): heappush(low, heappop(high)); // rebalance sizes so low is equal-or-one-bigger. findMedian(): if len(low) > len(high): return low.top (odd count, low holds the extra element); else return (low.top + high.top) / 2.0. This 'push-to-low, shuttle-top-to-high, rebalance-if-needed' order guarantees both invariants after every add without case analysis. Median is O(1) because both middle candidates are heap roots. Use floating-point or a+(b-a)/2 averaging to avoid overflow when summing two large middles.
pitfalls: Maintaining only the size invariant but not the ordering invariant (or vice versa) — the tops stop being the true middles.
Getting which heap holds the extra element wrong, so odd-count median comes from the wrong root.
Overflow when averaging two large middle values (use /2.0 or a + (b-a)/2).
Using a plain min-heap for the lower half — you need a max-heap (negate values if needed).
Re-sorting on every findMedian, which defeats the purpose for a heavy query stream.

interviewer_notes: The discriminator is whether the candidate moves past 'keep it sorted' to the two-heaps idea. If they start with a sorted array, accept it, then ask 'what's the cost per addNum, and can you make findMedian O(1)?' to pressure toward heaps. The subtle correctness point is that BOTH invariants (sizes within 1, and every-low <= every-high) must hold — a candidate who only balances sizes has a latent bug; probe by adding numbers out of order (e.g. add 5, then 1, then 3) and asking them to trace the heaps. Stay silent otherwise. Confirm even/odd median and overflow-safe averaging. For strong candidates, escalate: the bounded-range histogram optimization, then removeNum / sliding-window median (lazy deletion), and finally distributed approximate quantiles (t-digest) as a staff-level stretch.
